steps.say: A tumour on the balance nerve announces itself with deafness on one side, ringing and unsteadiness. The scan shows a bright lump shaped like an ice-cream cone, its tip sitting inside the ear canal. That canal-centred shape is the signature of this tumour.
steps.tx: Unilateral **sensorineural hearing loss** (one-sided nerve deafness) with tinnitus and imbalance is the classic triad. MRI shows an enhancing **ice-cream cone** (cone-shaped tumour) mass centred on the **internal auditory canal** (ear-canal tunnel) with canal flaring, a shape that separates schwannoma from other cerebellopontine angle lumps at a glance.

vis.alt: Anatomical illustration showing a vestibular schwannoma occupying the internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle, with an inset of Antoni A tissue and Verocay bodies.
vis.caption: Vestibular schwannoma filling the canal and angle, with Verocay bodies inset. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Surgeons stage these tumours from tiny ones hidden inside the canal to giants squashing the brainstem. The smallest grades stay inside the canal, while the largest press the breathing centres and shift fluid spaces. Higher stage is treated in a more complex way.
steps.tx: **Koos grades** (size and contact scale) run from **1** (one) to **4** (four), tracking size from purely **intracanalicular** (inside-the-canal) tumour to **brainstem compression** (brainstem squashing) with fourth ventricular shift. Grading guides observation versus treatment, since contact with the brainstem raises both surgical risk and the urgency to act.

steps.say: Hearing is measured on a standard scale before any decision, because useful hearing changes everything. When hearing still serves daily life, surgeons fight to preserve it. Without useful hearing, the priority shifts entirely to saving the face nerve.
steps.tx: **Gardner-Robertson** (hearing grading scale) classes record preoperative hearing, and **serviceable hearing** (useful aidable hearing) entering treatment decides the plan. **Hearing preservation** (keeping useful hearing) drives the choice between hearing-sparing retrosigmoid surgery, middle fossa surgery or focused radiation when hearing still serves.

steps.say: Small tumours in older patients are usually quiet for years, so doctors watch them with yearly scans. Most never grow at all. Only growth or pressure on the brainstem converts watching into treatment.
steps.tx: Lesions below **1.5 cm** (one point five centimetres) in the elderly are observed with **serial MRI** (yearly repeat scans) because most show no **growth** (size increase). New growth or brainstem compression converts **observation** (planned watching) to treatment, so surveillance continues for life even when the first years look quiet.

steps.say: Focused radiation beams control small tumours while keeping hearing better than surgery does. A single modest dose to the edge holds growth in most cases. The costs are delayed facial or trigeminal nerve injury and a tiny late risk of malignant change.
steps.tx: Stereotactic **radiosurgery** (focused beam treatment) with **12 Gy marginal dose** (twelve gray edge dose; 12 to **13 Gy** across tumours below **3 cm** (three centimetres)), controls disease with the best **hearing preservation** (kept useful hearing). The price is delayed facial or trigeminal nerve injury and rare malignant transformation, traded against avoiding open surgery.

steps.say: Three routes are used to reach this corner of the skull, each with a different sacrifice. The behind-the-ear route can keep hearing in bigger tumours, the through-the-ear route gives it up for the safest face outcome, and the above-the-ear route suits tiny canal tumours with good hearing.
steps.tx: Surgeons open behind the ear (**retrosigmoid**) when hearing can still be saved in bigger tumours, go through the ear (**translabyrinthine**) for the safest face result when hearing is already gone in large lesions, and open above the ear (**middle fossa**) for tiny canal tumours with good hearing. Route choice balances hearing against face-nerve safety.

steps.say: Keeping the face moving matters more than removing every last cell. When tumour clings to the face nerve, surgeons deliberately leave a scrap and finish it later with radiation. Chasing the final millimetre at the cost of a smile is never worth it.
steps.tx: **Facial nerve** (cranial nerve **7** (seven)) preservation outranks total removal, so **planned subtotal resection** (deliberate partial removal) leaves a **planned remnant** (deliberate scrap on the nerve) for radiosurgery in large tumours. Chasing total resection at the price of a permanent facial palsy trades cure for disfigurement.

steps.say: Tumours on both sides mean an inherited disease that needs family-wide thinking. A vessel antibody can sometimes restore hearing without surgery, and ears deafened by bilateral treatment can hear again through implants. Relatives need screening once the pattern appears.
steps.tx: **Bilateral schwannoma** (both-sided tumours) defines **NF2** (neurofibromatosis type 2), where **bevacizumab** (vessel antibody) can restore hearing without surgery. Ears deafened by bilateral treatment gain sound through a **cochlear implant** (inner-ear device) or brainstem implant, and relatives are screened once the inherited pattern is recognised.
